summary:
Over the course of this project, we have created a web application to explore and plan possible missions on the moon, specifically looking at the South Pole region. This was created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to provide insight into some of the issues that astronauts and mission planners face, such as lack of sunlight, rough terrain and communication issues.
This was achieved by creating an interactive 3D moon along with NASA's height information. This allows the user to view 5 set landing sites or choose their own site on our 3d moon. The application analyses the Sun and Earth visibility, local terrain obstructions to ensure the best mission windows. We have also included features to allow comparison of landing sites and estimation of energy production from solar panels, battery performance and distance travelled across the surface.
We wanted to create an all-in-one lunar mission planner rather than just another 3D moon viewer. The application allows users to play around with different locations and scenarios to gain a better insight into how the environment on the moon could impact a mission.
details:
There is a number of factors to consider when planning missions around the south pole of the Moon. For example, the sun will be very low, there may be long periods where the sun is obscured by other terrain features and the Earth will not be clearly visible. This can affect how much power you generate, what activities you can do and when communication can occur.

We created an application called LunarNav which shows people the difficulties associated with planning missions around the Moon. It allows users to look at a number of different points to consider when choosing where to go on the Moon. This can be done by either selecting one of the five set points or a custom point on our interactive 3D moon.

The application uses JavaScript to calculate an approximation of the sun and Earth positions at the selected point. It uses NASA height data to take into account any local obstructions. This means it can show how much light will be present, when there will be no light, when Earth will be in view and when both the sun and Earth will be in view. It also has a Mission Window Finder tool which looks for the best mission windows.

Users can easily compare points, see the height profile of the terrain, a 360° view of the terrain and get some basic engineering calculations such as solar generation, battery performance and distance travelled on the surface.

Note: The link to the live application is below and also in the github repository's README.md file:
https://firstlunarnav.web.app/


Benefits and Impact?
We wanted to help make some aspects of Lunar mission planning easier to understand. As there are some complex data to consider for lunar missions, it can be tricky to understand, especially if you don’t have a background in planetary science or engineering. We have included a variety of different analyses in one place to make it easy for the user.

We hope this can help students, teachers, space enthusiasts and anyone looking to understand more about lunar missions. Most importantly we want to make people aware that the landing site isn’t always the most important factor to consider. The local terrain, lighting and timing are all important. This could act as a starting point for someone wanting to do more in-depth research on mission planning.

Tools and Technology
Languages: JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3 and GLSL.
WebGL: To display our interactive 3D moon model, terrain and visualisations.
Data: LOLA height data, SLDEM2015 Lunar height data and LROC images from NASA. These were used to create our terrain models, local horizon calculations and lunar visualisation.
Calculations: Custom JavaScript models to calculate sun and Earth positions, visibility and mission windows.
Validation: We validated our sun and Earth position calculations by comparing them to 90 observations from NASA/JPL Horizons. We looked at three different points around the South pole and three different times.
GeoTIFF.js: To read in and process our height data.
AI: Google Gemini API to give our optional in-app AI assistant.
We also used Git, GitHub and VS Code.
The free version of the Gemini web interface was used for brainstorming, background research and repetitive support tasks. All of the core code and models were developed by us.

Creativity?
We didn’t want to create another 3D moon visualiser. Our main concept was to bring together astronomical visibility calculations with lunar terrain data. We have calculated whether the sun/Earth should be visible but also taken into account if they would be blocked by the local terrain.

We have linked this to mission window calculations and basic power calculations. This means users can see how changing a point and/or time can affect their mission. As we have given the option to select our own point it means the user does not have to use one of our five examples. We also have a 360° view of the terrain which makes it easier to understand.

Things Considered?
Mainly we wanted to consider how much sun there would be, if Earth would be in view, if there would be any communication opportunities, local terrain, power requirements and mission timing. We also wanted to ensure this application was easy to use for someone without any specialist knowledge. We have included visualisations, comparisons and simple explanations.

This is a prototype for research and education purposes. The astronomical calculations have been validated against JPL Horizons. The terrain and engineering models are based on simple assumptions and need to be validated further before they could be used in real missions.
